token-security.name: Token Security Scanner

faq.q: Can CRYPY tell me a token is safe?
faq.a: No. CRYPY shows the risks it could check and how each was checked. Passing checks don't prove a token is honest, and owners can change fees or trading later.

faq.q: How does the trade test work?
faq.a: CRYPY runs a small test contract inside a read-only call against the real exchange pool: it buys, sends some to another wallet and sells. Nothing is signed or sent, and no wallet is needed.

faq.q: What does "heuristic" mean?
faq.a: It was inferred from the contract's code, for example a mint function being present. It shows what is possible, not what has happened.

faq.q: Where do holder numbers come from?
faq.a: From GoPlus Security, an outside provider, shown with its name. CRYPY doesn't count holders on its own yet.

faq.q: Which chains and exchanges are covered?
faq.a: Ethereum and BNB Chain. The trade test uses Uniswap v2, PancakeSwap v2, SushiSwap and Biswap pools; liquidity is also read from Uniswap and PancakeSwap v3.

faq.q: Do I need to connect my wallet?
faq.a: No. Balances are public on the blockchain, so any address can be checked without connecting or signing anything.

faq.q: Where do the balances and prices come from?
faq.a: Balances are read from the blockchain itself. USD prices are also read on-chain, from PancakeSwap and Uniswap pools with enough liquidity (at least $5,000 on the quote side). Tokens without such a pool are listed but not counted in the total.

faq.q: Why are some tokens hidden?
faq.a: Scammers send worthless tokens to many wallets, often with a website in the name, to lure people to fake sites. CRYPY hides tokens that look like this and shows the reason. Never visit links in token names.

faq.q: Why does the value differ from my wallet app?
faq.a: Wallet apps may use other price sources, update at different times, or include tokens without a reliable on-chain price. CRYPY never guesses a price.

faq.q: Which chains are checked?
faq.a: Ethereum and BNB Chain. The same address can hold different coins and tokens on each chain, so both are shown.

faq.q: Do I need to connect my wallet?
faq.a: No. Transactions are public, so any hash can be checked without connecting or signing anything.

faq.q: Where does the information come from?
faq.a: Directly from blockchain nodes: the transaction, its receipt and its events. Prices are read from on-chain pools. Nothing is bought from a data provider.

faq.q: How sure is the explanation?
faq.a: Each explanation shows its evidence: confirmed on the blockchain, decoded from the transaction, or likely. When something can't be identified, CRYPY says so instead of guessing.

faq.q: Why can't I see why my old transaction failed?
faq.a: Reading the reason means replaying the transaction on the network state just before it. Free nodes keep that state only for recent blocks, so for older transactions the reason may not be available.

faq.q: Which networks are supported?
faq.a: Ethereum and BNB Chain. The table on this page shows exactly which parts work on each network.

unit-converter.name: Unit Converter
unit-converter.question: How many gwei is this?
unit-converter.description: Convert between wei, gwei and ETH or BNB exactly, without rounding.
features: Wei, gwei and ETH or BNB, both ways
Exact to the last wei, no rounding

howTo: Type an amount into any box: wei, gwei or ETH / BNB.
The other two boxes update instantly with the exact value.
Use the copy button next to a value to copy it.

faq.q: What is wei?
faq.a: Wei is the smallest unit of ETH: 1 ETH equals 1,000,000,000,000,000,000 wei (10^18). BNB on BNB Chain uses the same 18 decimals, so the same units apply to BNB.

faq.q: What is gwei?
faq.a: One gwei is 1,000,000,000 wei (10^9), or 0.000000001 ETH. Gas prices are usually quoted in gwei.

faq.q: How do I work out a transaction fee?
faq.a: Multiply the gas used by the gas price. For example, a simple transfer using 21,000 gas at 20 gwei costs 420,000 gwei, which is 0.00042 ETH.

faq.q: Do tokens use the same units?
faq.a: Not always. Many tokens use 18 decimals like ETH, but some don't: USDT on Ethereum uses 6 decimals, while USDT on BNB Chain uses 18. Check the token's decimals before converting token amounts.

faq.q: Is anything I type sent to a server?
faq.a: No. The conversion runs entirely in your browser.

hex-converter.name: Hex Converter
hex-converter.question: What number is this hex value?
hex-converter.description: Convert hexadecimal and decimal values used on blockchains, up to 256 bits.
features: Hex to decimal and back
32-byte form, byte length and signed reading
Shows text hidden in hex data
Runs in your browser
howTo: Paste a hex value (with or without 0x) or a decimal number.
See the decimal, hex and 32-byte forms instantly.
For digits-only input, choose whether it is decimal or hex.

faq.q: Why do blockchains use hex?
faq.a: The EVM works with 32-byte words, and node APIs return numbers such as block numbers, balances and gas in hexadecimal (for example 0x10 = 16).

faq.q: What is the 32-byte form?
faq.a: The value padded to 64 hex digits. This is how numbers appear in transaction data and contract storage.

faq.q: What is the signed value?
faq.a: Contracts can store signed numbers (int256) using two's complement. When a 32-byte value starts with the top bit set, it represents a negative number, shown here.

faq.q: What is the largest value supported?
faq.a: 2^256 − 1, the largest number an EVM uint256 can hold.

address-formatter.name: Address Formatter
address-formatter.question: Is this address written correctly?
address-formatter.description: Check that an address is written correctly and get its checksummed form. Works for one address or a list.
features: Detects typing mistakes using the EIP-55 checksum
Checks up to 500 addresses at once
Works for every EVM chain
Runs in your browser
howTo: Paste one address, or a list with one address per line.
Each address is marked as correct, unprotected (no checksum) or mistyped.
Copy the checksummed form of correct addresses.

faq.q: What is a checksum address?
faq.a: EIP-55 mixes upper- and lower-case letters in an address to encode a check. If you mistype a character, the check almost always fails, so the mistake is caught before you send anything.

faq.q: Is an all-lowercase address valid?
faq.a: Yes. It is the same address, but it carries no checksum, so a typing mistake could go unnoticed. The checksummed form adds that protection.

faq.q: What should I do if the checksum is wrong?
faq.a: Don't use the address. A wrong checksum means a character was changed. Copy the address again from its original source; don't try to fix it by hand.

faq.q: Is the address the same on Ethereum and BNB Chain?
faq.a: All EVM chains use the same address format, so the same address can exist on each of them, but balances and contracts differ per chain. Exchange deposit addresses often accept only one network, so always check which network the recipient supports.

faq.q: Does a correct address mean it is safe?
faq.a: No. It only means the address is written correctly. Use CRYPY's search to see what the address is before sending to it.

tx-decoder.name: Transaction Data Decoder
tx-decoder.question: What does this transaction data mean?
tx-decoder.description: Turn raw transaction data into a readable function and values, with warnings for risky approvals.
features: Decodes common token, NFT, router and ownership functions
Warns about unlimited approvals and NFT operator approvals
Decodes calls inside multicall
Runs in your browser
howTo: Copy the transaction's input data (it starts with 0x) from a block explorer or your wallet's data view.
Paste it here; it is decoded instantly.
Read the function, its values and any warnings before you confirm a transaction.

faq.q: What is transaction data?
faq.a: The input data tells a contract what to do. The first 4 bytes (the function selector) identify the function, and the rest holds its values in 32-byte words.

faq.q: Where do I find it?
faq.a: On a block explorer, open the transaction and look for Input Data (view it as the original hex). Many wallets also show the hex data in an advanced or data tab before you confirm.

faq.q: What is an unlimited approval?
faq.a: It lets the spender move any amount of that token from your wallet, now and in the future, until you revoke it. If the spender is malicious or later hacked, those tokens can be taken.

faq.q: Why does it say unknown function?
faq.a: CRYPY only decodes a list of well-known functions and never guesses. Different functions can share the same selector, so guessing could show you the wrong meaning.

faq.q: Why are amounts so large?
faq.a: Amounts are in the token's smallest unit. Divide by 10 to the power of the token's decimals, or use the Unit Converter for 18-decimal tokens.

howTo: Paste your addresses, one per line. Add a label after a comma if you like (0x…,Treasury), or upload a CSV/TXT file.

faq.q: Do I need to connect a wallet?
faq.a: No. Balances are public, so any list of addresses can be checked without connecting or signing anything. CRYPY never asks for keys or seed phrases.

faq.q: Is my list stored?
faq.a: No. Addresses are sent to CRYPY's server only to read their balances and are not stored or logged. Labels never leave your browser, and the list is never put in the page address.

faq.q: Where do the balances come from?
faq.a: Directly from blockchain nodes, all read at the same block. Prices come from on-chain DEX pools; tokens without a reliable price show amounts only.

faq.q: How many addresses can I check?
faq.a: Up to 500 addresses on up to 2 chains with up to 6 assets per scan. Very large lists, saved lists and scheduled re-scans are planned for later.

faq.q: Why does an address show as a contract?
faq.a: It has smart-contract code on that chain. Wallets that delegate to code (EIP-7702) are shown as delegated wallets.

privacy.title: Privacy Policy
body: CRYPY never asks for, collects or stores seed phrases, recovery phrases or private keys.
Addresses and transaction hashes you search are public blockchain data. CRYPY does not store them, except addresses you choose to save to a watchlist after signing in.
Your language and theme choices are saved in your browser only.
Full details, including any analytics and third-party services, will be listed here before launch.

terms.title: Terms of Use
body: CRYPY provides information tools for public blockchain data. It does not hold, move or manage your funds.
You are responsible for every transaction you confirm in your own wallet.
Full terms will be published here before launch.

risk.title: Risk Disclosure
body: Crypto assets are risky. Prices can fall to zero and transactions cannot be reversed.
CRYPY's security checks show signals from automated tools and data providers. No check can prove that a token, contract or wallet is safe.
Nothing on CRYPY is financial, legal or tax advice. Always do your own research.

pending.yes: Yes. The sender hasn't used this transaction's number (nonce {nonce}) for another transaction.
pending.no: No. The sender already used this transaction's number (nonce {nonce}) for another transaction, so this one was replaced or cancelled and can't confirm.
pending.unknown: We couldn't check this right now.

how.title: How we checked.
how.body: Pools were found on {dexes}, plus pools GoPlus lists once confirmed with their exchange's factory. Holders were found from known addresses (burn addresses, the owner, registered lockers, farms and fee collectors), GoPlus's list of the largest holders, recent LP transfers, and the lockers' own lists of locked v3 positions. Every share and every unlock date was then read from the blockchain. A locker counts only if it is in CRYPY's checked list (UNCX, PinkLock, Team Finance, OnlyMoons vaults); a contract that only calls itself a lock counts as unidentified. A lock protects only until its end date.

lock.until: Locked until {date} (in {days, plural, one {# day} other {# days}}).
lock.soon: Unlocks {date}, in {days, plural, one {# day} other {# days}}. Then it can be withdrawn.
lock.ended: Lock ended {date} ({days, plural, one {# day} other {# days}} ago) and wasn't withdrawn: it can be withdrawn at any moment.

control.multisig: {threshold} of {signers} signers must agree to remove it. They can still do that at any time.
control.multisigOne: A multisig where one signer (of {signers}) can remove it alone.
control.timelock: Any withdrawal must wait about {hours, plural, one {# hour} other {# hours}} (read from the contract), so it would be visible in advance.
control.farm: Staked by many people, not one holder.
control.exchange: The exchange's fee collector: it earns a small share of every pool.
control.owner: The token's owner can remove it at any time.
control.token: Held by the token's own contract. What it can do depends on that contract's code.
control.pool: Sent back to the pool; it goes with the next withdrawal.
control.wallet: Can be removed at any time.
control.contract: CRYPY can't tell whether this contract can release it. It is not in CRYPY's list of known lockers.
control.burn: Gone for good: nobody can withdraw it.
control.upgradeable: This lock contract can be upgraded by its operator, so the lock is only as safe as that operator.

approvals.title: Approvals
approvals.intro: An approval lets another address move your tokens without asking again. Revoke the ones you don't use, and any you don't recognise.

ui.readOnlyBody: Anyone can check any address. Revoking only works when the wallet that gave the approval is connected.
ui.attentionBody: They can move up to {usd} of your tokens right now.
ui.attentionBodyNoPrice: Check them and revoke the ones you don't recognise.
ui.noneAttentionBody: All approvals found go to known apps or contracts with published source. Revoke the ones you no longer use.
ui.noneFoundBody: No active approvals were found on {chains}. CRYPY searched GoPlus's list and its own checks; an approval it couldn't find wouldn't show here.
ui.revokeFlaggedNote: One wallet confirmation each · free apart from network fees
ui.groupAttentionNote: revoke these unless you are sure you need them
ui.groupNormalNote: known apps or contracts with published source: revoke the ones you no longer use
ui.groupCheckNote: unknown contracts: make sure each is an app you meant to use
ui.unlimitedNote: also covers tokens you receive later
ui.reasonMalicious: GoPlus lists this address as malicious. It can take your {symbol}, now and later.
ui.reasonWallet: This is a person's wallet, not an app. Apps never need this; it is a common way scams drain wallets.
ui.reasonUnknownContract: Its source isn't published and it isn't on CRYPY's list of known apps. Check it's an app you meant to use.
ui.reasonUnreadable: CRYPY couldn't read what this spender is. Check it before keeping the approval.
ui.reasonUnused: You hold no {symbol}, so nothing is at risk today. Safe to revoke if you no longer use it.
ui.how: Approvals were found with GoPlus's approval list and CRYPY's own checks (popular apps and Permit2 for every token you hold, and your approvals of the last few hours for those tokens). Every allowance shown was then read again from the blockchain. "At risk now" is the smaller of the allowance and what you hold, at on-chain prices. An approval CRYPY couldn't find isn't shown, so this list may be incomplete.
ui.howSafety: Revoking costs a small network fee and is signed in your own wallet. CRYPY never asks for your seed phrase or private key, and never sends anything without your click.
ui.goplusDown: GoPlus didn't answer on {chains}. Only CRYPY's own checks ran there (popular apps and Permit2 for the tokens you hold), so approvals to other spenders may be missing. Check again in a minute.
ui.chainDown: {chain} couldn't be read right now. Check again in a minute.
ui.batchNote: Revoking several in one transaction (batch revoke) is planned as a paid tool later. Single revokes and basic checks always stay free.
ui.dialogTested: CRYPY tested this exact transaction first: it succeeds and only sets this allowance to 0.
ui.dialogNotTested: CRYPY couldn't test this transaction right now, so it won't open your wallet. Try again in a minute.
ui.dialogMatch: Check the contract and function in your wallet match the ones above before you confirm.
ui.stepSwitching: Your wallet will ask you to switch network. Nothing is signed.
ui.stepPending: Waiting for the transaction to be included…
ui.stepVerifying: Reading the allowance again from the blockchain…
ui.doneNotCleared: The transaction went through, but the allowance didn't read as 0 yet. Check again in a minute.
ui.doneReadAgain: Read again from the blockchain at block {block}.
ui.queueNote: Each one is a separate transaction: your wallet asks for each, and you can stop at any time.
ui.wrongAccount: Only the wallet that gave the approval can revoke it. Your wallet is connected as {connected}; this page is about {owner}.
ui.wrongNetwork: This approval is on {chain}. Your wallet didn't switch to it, so nothing was sent.
ui.rejected: You rejected the request in your wallet. Nothing was sent and the approval is unchanged.
ui.testFailed: The test of this transaction failed, so CRYPY didn't open your wallet. The token may not allow changing approvals right now.
ui.failed: The transaction failed. The approval may be unchanged; check again before trying once more.
ui.groupSpamNote: tokens CRYPY hides as likely spam: nothing of value at risk
ui.reasonSpamToken: This token looks like spam (CRYPY hides it in balances), so nothing of value is at risk. Revoking is optional; never visit links in the token's name.
ui.reasonNewContract: This contract was created {days} days before your approval and isn't on CRYPY's list of known apps. New unknown contracts are a common way scams drain wallets: check it's an app you meant to use.
ui.goplusPartial: GoPlus sent a partial list on {chains}, which is common for busy wallets. CRYPY used it together with its own checks; some approvals may still be missing.
ui.reasonDisputed: GoPlus lists this address as malicious, but CRYPY's own list identifies it as {name}, an official contract. Phishing sites sometimes send approvals through official contracts, so revoke it if you don't remember approving it yourself.
ui.checkBody: None goes to a wallet or an address flagged as malicious, but these go to contracts CRYPY can't fully identify. Revoke the ones you don't recognise or no longer use.
ui.recentSkipped: Your approvals of the last few hours couldn't be searched on {chains} right now (the node was slow). Approvals found by the other checks are shown; check again in a minute.

activity.title: Activity
activity.intro: Every coin, token and NFT transfer to or from this address, newest first. Never copy an address from your history: scammers send look-alike transfers.

ui.recentOnly: Full history isn't available right now on {chains}, so only the last few hours of token transfers for tokens this wallet holds are shown (coin transfers can't be found that way). Check again later.
ui.chainDown: {chain} couldn't be read right now. Check again in a minute.
ui.empty: No transfers were found for this address on these chains.
ui.poisoning: Possible address poisoning: {sender} starts and ends like {lookalike}. Scammers send these so you copy the wrong address later. Never copy addresses from your history.
ui.how: Coin, token and NFT transfers to or from this address from Alchemy's free transfer history, newest first. "Value now" uses today's on-chain price, not the price at the time. Swaps are our reading of transfers in one transaction, labelled "Interpretation". Likely spam is hidden by default and never deleted.
ui.noInternal: On {chains}, coins moved inside contracts (internal transfers) aren't in our free source, so a payment from a contract may be missing.
ui.howRecent: Without the history source, CRYPY reads the last few hours of token transfers straight from the chain, only for tokens this wallet holds now.
